## About this course

-   How to analyse molecular data in R: from a table of numbers to a figure and a conclusion.
-   The statistical methods behind most analyses of molecular data: what they do and when to use them.
-   If time allows: working directly with sequencing results, e.g. assembling a mitochondrial genome.

## Course roadmap

1.  R and data visualization: R basics, ggplot2 (today: R basics)
2.  Statistical foundations: descriptive statistics, hypothesis testing, linear models, ANOVA, generalized linear models (GLM)
3.  Multivariate methods: PCA, nMDS, clustering; PERMANOVA if time allows
4.  Molecular applications: differential expression in RNA-seq, enrichment analysis
5.  If time allows: genome assembly

## How the course works

-   Each session: lecture + hands-on practice in R.
-   After each session: a Moodle quiz, required, to be completed before the next session, + optional tasks for bonus points.
-   AI tools: use them to understand errors and concepts, not to solve tasks for you.

## Today you will be able to

-   Set up R and RStudio and organise your course folder as an RStudio project
-   Find your way around the RStudio window and get help on functions
-   Create variables and vectors and select elements from them
-   Work with the main data types: numeric, character, logical, factors
-   Deal with missing values and write a simple function of your own
-   Store a data table in a data frame and select rows, columns and cells
-   Read a table from a CSV file and save one

# Getting started with R

## Download and install

Install **R** first, then **RStudio**, an **IDE** (integrated development environment) for R.

1.  **R**: open the Tsinghua University CRAN mirror (fast from China) <https://mirrors.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/CRAN/>, then `Download R for Windows -> base` and download the `.exe` installer. Run it and accept the default settings.
2.  **RStudio**: <https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/>, then download RStudio Desktop for Windows (`.exe`). Run it and accept the default settings.
3.  Start **RStudio** from the Start menu (not R): RStudio finds R by itself.

*macOS / Linux:* on macOS, download the R `.pkg` for your processor (Apple silicon or Intel) and the RStudio `.dmg`; on Linux, install R from your distribution's packages (e.g. `r-base` on Ubuntu) and the RStudio `.deb`/`.rpm`.

## Your course folder

1.  Create a folder for ALL course materials, e.g. `moldiveco` in `Documents`. This folder will be your **working directory**. Save ALL your code files (`.R`) here.
2.  Inside it, create a folder `data` for all data files.

You should end up with something like this:

    C:\Users\<your name>\Documents\moldiveco\
    C:\Users\<your name>\Documents\moldiveco\data\

-   Use only Latin letters, numbers and `_` in folder and file names: no spaces, no Chinese characters.
-   Windows hides file extensions by default. To see `.R` and `.Rproj`, turn them on in File Explorer: Windows 11: `View -> Show -> File name extensions`; Windows 10: `View` tab, tick `File name extensions`.

*macOS / Linux:* the folder is `/Users/<your name>/Documents/moldiveco/` (macOS) or `/home/<your name>/moldiveco/` (Linux); file extensions are shown in Finder via `Finder -> Settings -> Advanced`.

## The RStudio window

When you first open RStudio, it has four panes:

-   **Source** (top left): your scripts
-   **Console** (bottom left): R runs your commands here
-   **Environment / History** (top right): the objects you have created
-   **Files / Plots / Packages / Help** (bottom right)

## Console vs script

-   **Console**: R runs a command as soon as you press `Enter`. Good for quick checks, but nothing is saved.
-   **Script**: a text file with your code. Create one with `File -> New File -> R Script` (`Ctrl + Shift + N`). Save it with `Ctrl + S` into your course folder, e.g. `C:\Users\<your name>\Documents\moldiveco\01_intro.R`; then you can run the whole analysis again at any time.

Write all code you want to keep in a script.

*macOS:* `Cmd` instead of `Ctrl` (`Cmd + Shift + N`, `Cmd + S`).

## RStudio projects

In this course, always work inside an RStudio **project**: your course folder with a `.Rproj` file in it. RStudio then uses the project folder as the working directory, so you never have to set it by hand.

-   Create the project once: `File -> New Project -> Existing Directory`, then choose your `moldiveco` folder.
-   Every time you work: double-click `moldiveco.Rproj` in File Explorer. RStudio opens with the working directory already set.
-   Files inside the project are then found with short paths.
-   Keep all data files in `data/`, images and plots in `images/`, and scripts (`.R`) in the project folder itself. Then paths are always short and predictable, e.g. `"data/genes.csv"`.

*macOS / Linux:* double-click `moldiveco.Rproj` in Finder / your file manager.

## File paths on Windows

A **file path** is the address of a file or folder. File Explorer shows paths with backslashes: `C:\Users\student\Documents\moldiveco`. If you paste such a path into R as it is, you get an error, because inside R text `\` starts a special character (e.g. `\n` is a new line):

```{r}
#| eval: false
setwd("C:\Users\student\Documents\moldiveco")
# Error: '\U' used without hex digits in character string
```

In R, write Windows paths with `/` (recommended) or with a double backslash `\\`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
setwd("C:/Users/student/Documents/moldiveco")
setwd("C:\\Users\\student\\Documents\\moldiveco")
```

Inside an RStudio project you rarely need a full path: use a **relative path**, which starts from the working directory, e.g. `"data/genes.csv"`.

*macOS / Linux:* paths already use `/`, e.g. `/Users/student/Documents/moldiveco`, so you can paste them as they are.

## How to get help

1.  In RStudio, put the cursor on a function name, e.g. `setwd`, and press `F1`.
2.  Type a question mark before the function name and run the line: `?setwd`.
3.  Use the function `help()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| script: "comment"
help("setwd")
```

*macOS:* on a laptop keyboard you may need `Fn + F1`.

## Installing packages

A **package** adds new functions to R. Packages are downloaded from **CRAN**; choose a nearby CRAN mirror so that downloads are fast.

-   `Tools -> Global Options -> Packages -> Primary CRAN repository`: choose a mirror in China (e.g. Tsinghua).
-   Or run once per session: `options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://mirrors.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/CRAN/"))`

Install a package once (`install.packages()` or the `Install` button in the `Packages` pane); load it every time you start R with `library()`. More on this below, with tibbles.

On Windows, CRAN gives ready-to-use packages. They are saved in your personal library, e.g. `C:\Users\<your name>\AppData\Local\R\win-library\<R version>`; `.libPaths()` shows where.

*macOS / Linux:* macOS also gets ready-to-use packages; on Linux, packages are compiled from source, so installation is slower and some packages need extra system libraries.

## Comments

**Comments** in code start with the `#` symbol.

```{r}
# this is a comment, R will not run it
```

## Useful RStudio keyboard shortcuts

-   `Ctrl + Shift + N`: new script; `Ctrl + S`: save the script.
-   `Ctrl + Enter`: send the current line from the script to the console; if several lines are selected, all of them are run.
-   `Ctrl + Shift + Enter`: run the whole script.
-   `Ctrl + Shift + C`: comment/uncomment the selected lines.
-   `Alt` + drag the mouse: select a rectangular block of text (several lines at once).
-   `Tab` or `Ctrl + Space`: press after you start typing a function or variable name to get a list of suggestions. This helps you type faster and with fewer mistakes.
-   `Ctrl + L`: clear the console.
-   `Alt + -`: type the assignment operator (`<-`).
-   `Ctrl + Shift + M`: type the pipe operator `%>%`. We start using it on Nov 2; it needs the `dplyr` package (part of `tidyverse`).

*macOS:* `Cmd` instead of `Ctrl`, and `Option` instead of `Alt` (but `Ctrl + L` and `Ctrl + Space` stay the same).

## Type code with English input

R understands only "half-width" (English) symbols. Brackets, commas and quotation marks typed with a Chinese input method look similar, but they are different characters, and R stops with an error:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| purl: false
#| out-width: "95%"
#| out-height: "86%"
#| fig-cap: "Full-width brackets and commas: R stops with unexpected input."
screenshot_placeholder("images/fullwidth_error.png",
                       "Full-width brackets and commas: unexpected input error")
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
c(2, 4, 6) # half-width: works
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: false
#| script: "comment"
c（2，4，6） # full-width: Error: unexpected input
c(2, 4, 6) # half-width: works
```

If R reports `unexpected input` in a line that looks correct, retype its brackets, commas and quotation marks in English input.

## R as a calculator

R can do arithmetic with **operators** (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^`) and with functions such as `sqrt()`; `:` makes a sequence of numbers. Operators, functions and vectors are explained in the next slides.

```{r}
2+2
1024/2
1:10
34*4
2^4
sqrt(27)
```

## Variables

The **assignment operator** is the arrow `<-`. It (usually) works from right to left: the value of the expression on the right is stored in the object on the left. Type it with `Alt + -`.

`=` also works for assignment (`x = 5`), but in this course we use `<-`. `=` is used inside functions to give arguments, e.g. `seq(from = 1, to = 5)`.

A **variable** is a container: you can put different data and even functions into it. Anything stored in R under a name is an **object**.

Variable names can contain upper- and lower-case Latin letters, dots (`.`), underscores (`_`) and numbers, and must start with a letter. Choose clear, meaningful names.

```{r}
var_1 <- 1024 / 2
1238 * 3 -> var_2
var_2
```

*macOS:* `Option + -` types `<-`.

## How to name a variable?

-   `a`: bad, and so are `b`, `c` or `x`. Sometimes acceptable, though :)
-   `var1`: bad, but better
-   `var_1`: bad, but better
-   `seqlength`: meaningful, but hard to read
-   `seq_length`, `gc_content` or `read_count`: good, meaningful and easy to read

The Environment pane shows all the objects you have created.

## Vectors

R can store data in different kinds of objects. R is a vector language: most objects in R are vectors.

There are two kinds of vectors:

-   atomic vectors: all elements have the same data type;
-   lists: elements can have different types.

Examples of atomic vectors:

```{r}
23
sqrt(25)
```

These are vectors of length 1: a single value is also a vector.

A **vector** is one object that holds one or more values, all of the same type.

## Some ways to create vectors

-   The `:` operator creates integer vectors with consecutive values.

```{r}
1:10 # from 1 to 10
-5:3 # from -5 to 3
```

-   The **function** `seq()` creates sequences of numbers.

```{r}
seq(from = 1, to = 5, by = 0.5)
```

`seq()` is a function, and `from`, `to` and `by` are its **arguments**. Functions and arguments are explained in more detail later.

## Some ways to create vectors

-   The function `c()` (from "concatenate").

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| script: "comment"
?c # read the help page for this function
```

The function `c()` takes any number of arguments separated by commas and puts them together into a vector.

```{r}
c(2, 4, 6)
c(-9.3, 0, 2.17, 21.3)
```

Vectors can be stored in variables to use later

```{r}
vect_num <- -11:12 # numeric vector from -11 to 12, stored in vect_num
```

## Indexing vectors

With the `[]` operator, you can get some elements of a vector. Inside the square brackets, give the position numbers (the **index**) of one or several elements.

```{r}
vect_num[1] # the first element of vect_num
vect_num[10] # the 10th element
vect_num[22]
```

## Indexing vectors

To get several elements, give their positions as a vector. For example, to get elements 3 to 5, we need a vector that contains 3, 4 and 5:

```{r}
3:5
```

If we put it in square brackets, we get the elements at these positions

```{r}
vect_num[3:5]
```

## Selecting elements from a vector

In the same way, if the elements you need are not next to each other, give a vector of their positions made with `c()`. `c(2, 4, 6)` is a vector containing 2, 4 and 6, so

```{r}
vect_num[c(2, 4, 6)] # returns the 2nd, 4th and 6th elements
vect_num[c(1, 10, 20)] # returns the 1st, 10th and 20th elements
```

## Why does this give an error?

We want the 1st, 3rd and 5th elements, so we list them inside the square brackets:

```{r}
#| eval: false
vect_num[1, 3, 5]
```

Why does this give an error?

## Why does this give an error? Answer

```{r}
#| error: true
vect_num[1, 3, 5]
```

Inside `[ ]`, commas separate dimensions: rows and columns of a table (coming later). A vector has only one dimension, so its positions must be combined into one vector with `c()`:

```{r}
vect_num[c(1, 3, 5)] # correct
```

## Combining vectors

The function `c()` can combine several vectors into one

```{r}
c(1, 1, 5:9)
c(vect_num, vect_num)
c(100, vect_num)
```

Getting elements 1, 3, 5 and 22 to 24

```{r}
vect_num[c(1, 3, 5, 22:24)]
```

# Data types in R

## Numeric data

The **data type** of everything you saw in the previous section is **numeric**. R stores numbers in two ways:

-   **integer**: whole numbers, e.g. the numbers made by `:`;
-   **double**: numbers that can have a decimal part. Every number you type, even `5`, is stored as a double.

The function `class()` tells you what kind of data an object holds:

```{r}
class(1:10)
class(2.17)
class(5)
```

`class()` shows doubles simply as `"numeric"`. For calculations the difference almost never matters.

## Character data

Each text element (a "string", or **character** value) must be surrounded by quotation marks. Double and single quotes work the same; use one kind inside the other when the text contains quotes, e.g. `"it's"` or `'the "A" allele'`.

```{r}
"this is text"
'this is text, too'
```

Text values can be combined into a character vector.

```{r}
dna_seq <- c("A", "T", "G", "C", "T", "A") # a short DNA fragment
dna_seq # the whole vector
```

## Selecting from a character vector

Getting the first and the last elements. We know that here there are 6 elements.

```{r}
dna_seq[c(1, 6)]
```

Getting elements 5 to 10. `dna_seq` has only 6 elements, so first we glue a longer vector from two copies of it.

```{r}
double_seq <- c(dna_seq, dna_seq)
double_seq
double_seq[5:10] # elements 5 to 10
```

## Logical data

```{r}
TRUE # true
FALSE # false
```

**Logical** values can be shortened to their first capital letters. **But better don't do this**: the code is easier to read in full.

```{r}
c(T, T, T, T, F, F, T, T)
```

Creating a logical vector.

```{r}
c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)
```

One more logical vector

```{r}
short_logical_vector <- c(FALSE, TRUE)
```

## A vector holds one data type

If you mix types in one vector, R converts all values to one type, in the order logical -> numeric -> character:

```{r}
c(1, "A") # a number and text: everything becomes text
class(c(1, "A"))
c(1, TRUE) # a number and a logical: TRUE becomes 1
class(c(1, TRUE))
```

## Long vectors

To create long vectors of repeated elements, use the function `rep()`.

```{r}
rep(x = 1, times = 3) # 1 is repeated 3 times
rep(x = "A", times = 5) # "A" is repeated 5 times (a poly-A tail!)
rep(x = TRUE, times = 2) # TRUE is repeated 2 times
```

## What is a function?

A function is a named command that does something. You call it by its name with round brackets: `name(...)`.

The arguments are the inputs inside the brackets. Each is written `name = value`, and arguments are separated by commas. Some arguments have default values, so you can leave them out.

```{r}
rep(x = "A", times = 5) # function rep(), arguments x and times
```

## Function arguments

In R, you can leave out the names of function arguments if you give them in the order listed in the help page of the function.

```{r}
rep(TRUE, 5) # TRUE repeated 5 times, arguments without names
```

Let's create a logical vector where TRUE is repeated 3 times, FALSE 3 times and TRUE 4 times, and store it in the variable `vect_log`.

```{r}
vect_log <- c(rep(TRUE, 3), rep(FALSE, 3), rep(TRUE, 4))
vect_log
```

## Logical operators

**Logical operators** compare values or combine conditions. The result is a logical vector: `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each element.

```{=latex}
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\hline
Operator & Meaning & Example\\
\hline
\texttt{>} & greater than & \texttt{vect\_num > 0}\\
\texttt{<} & less than & \texttt{vect\_num < -5}\\
\texttt{>=} & greater than or equal to & \texttt{vect\_num >= 8}\\
\texttt{<=} & less than or equal to & \texttt{vect\_num <= -8}\\
\texttt{==} & equal to & \texttt{double\_seq == "G"}\\
\texttt{!=} & not equal to & \texttt{double\_seq != "A"}\\
\texttt{!} & not: turns \texttt{TRUE} into \texttt{FALSE} and back & \texttt{!(double\_seq == "G")}\\
\texttt{\&} & and: both conditions are \texttt{TRUE} & \texttt{vect\_num > 0 \& vect\_num < 5}\\
\texttt{|} & or: at least one condition is \texttt{TRUE} & \texttt{vect\_num < -10 | vect\_num > 10}\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
```

## Using logical vectors to filter data

Logical vectors made with logical operators can be used for **filtering** data.

Remember our character vector:

```{r}
double_seq
```

## Example 1

Getting only the guanines (`"G"`).

We can create a logical vector that is TRUE only for the 3rd and 9th elements.

```{r}
f_g <- double_seq == "G"
f_g
```

We can use this logical vector as a filter to get data from `double_seq`

```{r}
double_seq[f_g]
```

## Example 2

Getting all G and C from `double_seq` (to count the GC content). We already have the G filter, so we create a filter for C.

```{r}
f_c <- double_seq == "C"
```

"G or C" can be written with the logical "or" (`|`).

```{r}
f_g | f_c
```

Done: we have extracted all G and C.

```{r}
double_seq[f_g | f_c]
```

## A shorter way to write it

The same thing can be written in a shorter way.

In one line, very hard to read:

```{r}
double_seq[double_seq == "G" | double_seq == "C"]
```

With a separate filter, easier to read:

```{r}
f_gc <- double_seq == "G" | double_seq == "C"
double_seq[f_gc]
```

## The same filter in the tidyverse

The **tidyverse** is a collection of packages for data work, including `tibble`, `dplyr` and `ggplot2`. A preview of the same G/C filter with `filter()` from `dplyr`, on a data frame (a table, explained later):

```{r}
library(dplyr) # part of the tidyverse
filter(data.frame(base = double_seq), base %in% c("G", "C"))
```

We will use the tidyverse from Nov 2. The book uses the pipe `|>`; in this course we use `%>%`, which works the same way.

Wickham H., Çetinkaya-Rundel M., Grolemund G. (2023). *R for Data Science*, 2nd ed. O'Reilly. Free online: <https://r4ds.hadley.nz>.

## GC content from a logical vector

In calculations, `TRUE` counts as 1 and `FALSE` as 0. So `sum()` of a logical vector counts the `TRUE` values, and `mean()` gives their proportion.

```{r}
f_gc
sum(f_gc) # number of G and C bases
mean(f_gc) # GC content: the proportion of G and C, 4 of 12 bases
```

The operator `%in%` checks whether each value is one of several values: a shorter way to write the same filter.

```{r}
f_gc2 <- double_seq %in% c("G", "C")
mean(f_gc2)
```

## Example 3

We had a numeric vector.

```{r}
vect_num
```

Getting only the values greater than 0 from `vect_num`.

```{r}
vect_num[vect_num > 0]
```

Getting from `vect_num` all numbers that are either less than or equal to -8, or greater than or equal to 8.

```{r}
f_min8_plus8 <- (vect_num <= -8) | (vect_num >= 8)
vect_num[f_min8_plus8]
```

## Factors

A **factor** is the R object for discrete (= **categorical**) data. A factor defines the categories of a variable as a fixed set of levels: R knows which values are allowed and in which order the groups come. Factors are built on integer vectors and have extra attributes (`class` and `levels`).

For example, you genotyped 8 individuals at one SNP (a single-nucleotide polymorphism) with the alleles A and G. There are many individuals, but only three possible genotypes.

```{r}
snp_genotypes <- c("AG", "AA", "AA", "AA", "GG", "GG", "GG", "GG")
snp_genotypes # this is a character vector
```

"GG" means the same thing for every individual: genotype is a variable with three possible categories. A factor stores each value as a number matched with a label (called a **level**): the genotype name. Later in the course, statistical models (ANOVA, GLM) use factors to compare groups, so categorical predictors must be factors. We can create the factor "genotype".

## Creating a factor

```{r}
factor(snp_genotypes)
```

The levels of this factor are

-   1: AA,
-   2: AG,
-   3: GG.

By default, R sorts the levels alphabetically. You can change the order (see `help("factor")`). We will need this later.

```{r}
double_seq # character vector
```

Creating a factor from a character vector and storing it in a variable

```{r}
f_double_seq <- factor(double_seq)
```

## What kind of data is stored in a variable?

To find out what kind of data is stored in a variable, use the function `class()`

```{r}
class(f_double_seq)
class(vect_log)
class(vect_num)
class(dna_seq)
```

## Built-in constants in R

Built-in constants in R: `NA`, `NULL`, `NaN`, `Inf`

-   **NA**: "not available". The object exists, but its property was not measured or recorded.
-   **NULL**: empty, there is simply nothing.
-   **NaN**: "not a number".
-   **Inf**: "infinity".

```{r}
dna_seq_1 <- c("A", "T", NA, "C", "T", "A") # NA: 3rd base not read
length(NULL) # NULL: nothing, so no elements
0 / 0 # NaN
1 / 0 # Inf
```

## An element that does not exist

What happens if you ask for an element number that does not exist?

. . .

R returns NA, because there is no such element.

```{r}
dna_seq_1[198]
```

## Arithmetic with vectors

Operations work element by element: `vect_num + 2` adds 2 to every element.

```{r}
vect_num

vect_num + 2
vect_num * 2
```

## Arithmetic with vectors

```{r}
vect_num * (-2)
vect_num^2
```

Two vectors of the same length are combined position by position:

```{r}
c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20, 30)
```

## Operations on vectors with constants

```{r}
counts_na <- c(1, 3, NA, 7, 0, 22:24)
```

What happens to NA?

```{r}
counts_na + 2 # NA stays NA
counts_na * 0 # NA stays NA
counts_na / 0  # NA stays NA
```

*But in the last case you will also see:*

-   Inf when a number is divided by zero;
-   NaN when zero is divided by zero.

You also get NaN if you take the square root of a negative number.

```{r}
sqrt(-1)
```

## Functions in R

You have already seen many functions: you can recognise them by the brackets after the name. Let's meet a few more and learn to write our own functions. Your own functions let you automate repeated steps and make code easy to read.

Here is our vector

```{r}
counts_na
```

The length of a vector is given by the function `length()`

```{r}
length(counts_na)
```

The sum of its elements, with the function `sum()`

```{r}
sum(counts_na)
```

Oops! For some reason we got `NA`.

## Functions and vectors with constants

The function `sum()` has the argument `na.rm`, which is `FALSE` by default: NAs are not removed before the sum is calculated, so the result is NA.

If we give `sum()` the argument `na.rm = TRUE`, we get the correct sum

```{r}
sum(counts_na, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The same is true for `mean()`, and for `max()` and `min()` (the largest and the smallest value)

```{r}
mean(counts_na, na.rm = TRUE)
max(counts_na, na.rm = TRUE) # the largest value
min(counts_na, na.rm = TRUE) # the smallest value
```

## User-defined functions

Let's write our own function `mmean()` that calculates the mean of a vector and ignores missing values (`NA`) by default. This is a **user-defined function**.

```{r}
mmean <- function(x){
  mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  }
```

In this code:

-   `mmean` is a variable, the name of the function.
-   We store in it the function created by `function()`, a function that makes functions. The brackets list the arguments (names of the objects we give to the function to work with).
-   `{ }`: the curly brackets contain the body of the function: the steps to perform with the arguments.

## Return in the function body

Larger functions often also have the instruction `return()`, which says what exactly the function should return. This is how our function looks with it.

```{r}
mmean <- function(x){
  res <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  return(res)
}
```

Let's check our function on the vector with NA, against the built-in one

```{r}
mean(counts_na) # without na.rm: NA
mean(counts_na, na.rm = TRUE)
mmean(counts_na) # our function ignores NA by default
```

## Matrices

A **matrix** is a two-dimensional object, similar to an atomic vector but with the extra attribute `dim`.

For example, a small count matrix: how many sequencing reads came from each of 3 genes (rows) in each of 3 samples (columns). R fills the matrix column by column.

```{r}
counts <- matrix(c(1520, 980, 12, 1385, 1043, 30, 1610, 875, 7),
                 nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
rownames(counts) <- c("ACTB", "GAPDH", "MYC")
colnames(counts) <- c("sample_1", "sample_2", "sample_3")
counts
```

The dimensions of a matrix are set by two arguments: `nrow` (number of rows) and `ncol` (number of columns).

## Matrices: row and column names

`rownames()` and `colnames()` give names to the rows and columns of a matrix:

```{r}
rownames(counts)
colnames(counts)
```

The row names are real human gene symbols. *ACTB* (beta-actin) and *GAPDH* are **housekeeping genes**: they are needed in almost every cell and have high, stable expression. *MYC* is a regulatory gene, usually expressed at lower levels. The counts themselves are invented.

## Lists

A **list** is a data format where each element can be of any type and any length.

```{r}
my_list <- list(
  12:16,
  snp_genotypes,
  c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)
)

str(my_list)
```

## Data frames: two-dimensional data structures

A **data frame** is one of the ways to store tables in R. It is built on lists and also has some properties of matrices. It has the attributes `rownames` (row names) and `colnames` (column names). The `names` of a data frame are the same as its `colnames`.

Let's create a data frame. First, we create vectors with data for the variables.

```{r}
ids <- c("gene01", "gene02", "gene03", "gene04", "gene05",
         "gene06", "gene07", "gene08", "gene09") # character: gene IDs
exons <- c(9, 5, 1, 14, 8, 4, 3, 21, 11) # numeric: number of exons
strand <- c("+", "-", "-", "+", "+", "-", "+", "-", "-") # character: strand
# numeric: gene length, bp
len_bp <- c(5230, 18740, 960, 9410, 61200, 2870, 13350, 27600, 7980)
```

## Creating a data frame

Now we put these vectors into a data frame

```{r}
my_genes <- data.frame(gene_id = ids, n_exons = exons, length_bp = len_bp,
                       strand = strand)
```

We can check that we really created an object of class data.frame

```{r}
class(my_genes) # check that it is really a data frame
```

## Converting other objects to a data frame

For example, from a matrix...

```{r}
counts_data <- as.data.frame(counts)
str(counts_data)
```

## Looking at a data frame

There are several ways to look at the contents of a data frame.

```{r}
#| results: "hide"
my_genes # print the data frame
head(my_genes)
tail(my_genes)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| script: "comment"
View(my_genes) # spreadsheet view in RStudio
# fix(my_genes) # manual editing: avoid it, it leaves no record
```

You can also get the number of rows and columns of a data frame.

```{r}
nrow(my_genes)
ncol(my_genes)
length(my_genes) # gives the number of columns
```

## Indexing in data frames

Getting a column (variable) with the `$` operator and the variable name

```{r}
my_genes$n_exons
my_genes$length_bp
```

## Indexing in data frames

Each cell in a data frame has coordinates `[row, column]`

```{r}
my_genes[2, 3] # 2nd row, 3rd column
my_genes[2, ] # the whole 2nd row
my_genes[1:9, 2] # rows 1 to 9 of the 2nd column
my_genes[, 2] # the whole 2nd column
```

## Expanding a data frame

Adding a column.

```{r}
my_genes$chrom <- c("chr1", "chr1", "chr2", "chr3", "chr2",
                    "chr3", "chrX", "chr2", "chr3")
my_genes
```

## Adding a row

```{r}
my_genes_new <- data.frame(gene_id = "gene10", n_exons = 5,
                           length_bp = 1840, strand = "+", chrom = "chr1")
my_genes_final <- rbind(my_genes, my_genes_new)
my_genes_final
```

2.  Get the IDs of all genes on the minus strand (`"-"`).

## Tibbles

A **tibble** is a slightly modified data frame with a similar structure; it is a newer addition to R. Unlike data frames, tibbles have the extra class `tbl_df`, which makes them behave a little differently. Tibbles come from the package `tibble`, part of the tidyverse.

You install a package into your local library only once. So the `install.packages()` line should not stay in the final version of your script.

```{r}
# install.packages("tidyverse")
```

In each R session, you must load a package before you use it. Next time you start R, you will have to load the packages again. So the lines that load packages with `library()` must stay in the final version of your script.

```{r}
library(tibble)
my_tibble <- tibble(gene_id = ids, n_exons = exons,
                    length_bp = len_bp, strand = strand)
str(my_tibble)
```

## Tibbles

One difference between tibbles and data frames is how they are created. When you create a tibble, you can already use a column you have just created. Here `length_kb` is calculated from `length_bp` (`data.frame()` cannot do this):

```{r}
my_tibble2 <- tibble(gene_id = ids, length_bp = len_bp,
                     length_kb = length_bp / 1000, strand = strand)
my_tibble2
```

The tidyverse packages (e.g. `dplyr`, `ggplot2`) are built to work with tibbles. Tibbles also respond differently to some functions.

# Reading and writing data

## Reading a CSV file

A **CSV file** is a plain-text table: one row per line, values separated by commas. Save `genes.csv` (made-up practice data) into the `data` folder of your course project, then read it:

```{r}
genes <- read.csv("data/genes.csv")
head(genes)
```

`"data/genes.csv"` is a relative path: R looks for the file inside the working directory, i.e. your project folder. If R says `cannot open file ... No such file or directory`, check that you opened the project and that the file is in `data`.

## Checking what you have read

Always check the structure of a table you have just read:

```{r}
str(genes)
```

`read.csv()` returns a data frame: 15 observations (genes) of 6 variables. Text columns are character, numbers are integer or numeric (double).

## Writing a CSV file

Select the genes longer than 20 kb: a logical vector in the row position, and an empty column position (= all columns).

```{r}
long_genes <- genes[genes$length_bp > 20000, ]
long_genes
```

Save them into a new file in `data`. `row.names = FALSE` stops R from adding a column with row numbers.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| script: "comment"
write.csv(long_genes, "data/long_genes.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

The file appears in `data/` and in the `Files` pane; Excel can open it.

## What we have learned

-   **R** runs your code; **RStudio** is the IDE where you write it. Keep your code in a **script** and open your course folder as an RStudio **project**, so the **working directory** is set for you. In Windows paths, write `/` instead of `\`.
-   Anything stored in R under a name is an **object**. The **assignment operator** `<-` stores a value in a **variable**.
-   A **vector** is an ordered set of values of the same **data type**: numeric, character or logical. Select its elements by **index** (`x[3]`) or by **filtering** with a logical vector (`x[x > 0]`); `mean()` of a logical vector is a proportion, e.g. the GC content.
-   A **factor** stores a categorical variable with a fixed set of **levels**. **NA** is a missing value: many functions return NA unless you set `na.rm = TRUE`.
-   A **data frame** stores a data table: each column is a vector (one variable), each row is one observation. Select from it with `$` and `[row, column]`.
-   Read a table with `read.csv()` and save one with `write.csv()`, using **relative paths** inside the project. A **package** adds new functions: install it once, load it with `library()` every time you start R.

## Key R objects and functions: objects

\scriptsize

| Object | What it is | Example |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------|
| vector | An ordered set of one or more values, all of the same type | `c("A", "T", "G", "C")` |
| factor | A categorical variable; each value is one of a fixed set of levels | `factor(c("AG", "AA", "GG"))` |
| matrix | A two-dimensional table of values of one type | `matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)` |
| list | Holds elements of different types and lengths | `list(12:16, c(TRUE, FALSE))` |
| data frame | A data table: each column is a vector (one variable), all columns have the same length | `data.frame(gene_id = c("gene01", "gene02"), strand = c("+", "-"))` |
| tibble | A modern version of a data frame (package `tibble`, part of the tidyverse) | `tibble(n_exons = 1:3)` |

## Key R objects and functions: setup and vectors

\scriptsize

| Function | What it does | Example |
|------------|------------|-------------------------|
| `<-` | Stores a value in a variable | `x <- c(2, 4, 6)` |
| `=` | Gives a value to a function argument | `seq(from = 1, to = 5)` |
| `help()`, `?` | Opens the help page of a function | `?seq` |
| `setwd()` | Sets the working directory | `setwd("C:/Users/student/Documents")` |
| `install.packages()` | Installs a package (once) | `install.packages("tidyverse")` |
| `library()` | Loads a package (every R session) | `library(tibble)` |
| `c()` | Combines values into a vector | `c(-9.3, 0, 2.17)` |
| `:` | Integer sequence with step 1 | `1:10` |
| `seq()` | Sequence of numbers with any step | `seq(from = 1, to = 5, by = 0.5)` |
| `rep()` | Repeats values | `rep(x = "A", times = 5)` |
| `[ ]` | Selects elements by index or by a logical filter | `x[c(1, 3)]`, `x[x > 0]` |

## Key R objects and functions: working with vectors

\scriptsize

| Function | What it does | Example |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------|
| `==`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, `!`, `&`, &#124; | Logical operators: compare values, combine conditions (not, and, or) | `x == "G"`, `x > 0 & x < 8` |
| `%in%` | Is each value one of several values? | `x %in% c("G", "C")` |
| `filter()` | (`dplyr`, preview) Keeps the rows of a table that meet a condition | `filter(data.frame(base = x), base == "G")` |
| `factor()` | Turns a vector into a factor | `factor(snp_genotypes)` |
| `class()` | Shows what kind of object a variable holds | `class(dna_seq)` |
| `length()` | Number of elements in a vector | `length(x)` |
| `sum()` | Sum of the elements; `na.rm = TRUE` ignores NA | `sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)` |
| `mean()` | Arithmetic mean; `na.rm = TRUE` ignores NA; of a logical vector: a proportion | `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`, `mean(f_gc)` |
| `max()`, `min()` | Largest / smallest value; `na.rm = TRUE` ignores NA | `max(x, na.rm = TRUE)` |
| `sqrt()` | Square root | `sqrt(27)` |
| `function()` | Creates a user-defined function | `double_it <- function(x){ x * 2 }` |
| `return()` | Says what a function returns | `return(res)` |

## Key R objects and functions: tables and plots

\scriptsize

| Function | What it does | Example |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------|
| `matrix()` | Creates a matrix; `nrow`, `ncol` set its size | `matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)` |
| `rownames()`, `colnames()` | Names of rows / columns; can also set them | `rownames(counts) <- c("ACTB", "GAPDH", "MYC")` |
| `list()` | Creates a list | `list(12:16, snp_genotypes)` |
| `data.frame()` | Creates a data frame from vectors | `data.frame(n_exons = exons, strand = strand)` |
| `as.data.frame()` | Converts another object to a data frame | `as.data.frame(counts)` |
| `nrow()`, `ncol()` | Number of rows / columns | `nrow(my_genes)` |
| `$`, `[row, column]` | Selects a column; selects cells | `my_genes$n_exons`, `my_genes[2, 3]` |
| `rbind()` | Adds rows to a data frame | `rbind(my_genes, my_genes_new)` |
| `tibble()` | Creates a tibble | `tibble(n_exons = exons, strand = strand)` |

## Key R objects and functions: data files and plots

\scriptsize

| Function | What it does | Example |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------|
| `read.csv()` | Reads a CSV file into a data frame | `genes <- read.csv("data/genes.csv")` |
| `write.csv()` | Saves a data frame as a CSV file; `row.names = FALSE` drops the row numbers | `write.csv(long_genes, "data/long_genes.csv", row.names = FALSE)` |
| `str()` | Shows the structure of an object | `str(genes)` |
| `head()`, `tail()`, `View()` | First rows, last rows, a spreadsheet view | `head(genes)` |
| `hist()`, `plot()` | Quick histogram; quick scatterplot | `hist(genes$length_bp)` |
